stem.text:
(inli)

Gabrielle listens to her radio at a sound level of 80 dB . She attended a music concert that had a

sound level of 115 dB . Determine how many times more intense the music concert was than

the radio.

You may use the formula:

\[ \beta=10 \log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right) \]

where \(\quad \beta\) is the intensity level of sound, measured in dB

\(I\) is the intensity of sound

\(I_{0}\) is the standard minimum intensity that a person can hear

\[ 2(7)^{x}=3^{2 x-3} \]

stem.text:
In the binomial expansion of \(\left(\frac{7}{x^{3}}-3 x^{7}\right)^{n}\), the \(5^{\text {th }}\) term contains \(x^{7}\).

Determine the value of \(n\).

extensions.latexSource:
In the binomial expansion of \(\left(\frac{7}{x^{3}}-3 x^{7}\right)^{n}\), the \(5^{\text {th }}\) term contains \(x^{7}\).

Determine the value of \(n\).

solution.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} x^{7}  =\left(\frac{1}{x^{3}}\right)^{n-4}\left(x^{7}\right)^{4} \\ x^{7}  =\left(x^{-3}\right)^{n-4}\left(x^{7}\right)^{4} \\ x^{7}  =x^{-3 n+12+28} \\ 7  =-3 n+40 \\ -33  =-3 n \\ 11  =n \end{aligned} \]

1 mark for \(k=4\)

\(\frac{1}{2}\) mark for substitution

\(\frac{1}{2}\) mark for solving for \(n\)
